title: Opposition Stops the Rebuilding
overview: When the returned exiles start rebuilding the temple, neighbors they turn away work against them for years, and the chapter gathers several episodes of this opposition, some from much later times.

parts.label: Help offered and refused (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: The people offering help were descendants of groups the Assyrian kings had resettled in the old northern kingdom, and older accounts say they worshiped Israel's God alongside other gods. The leaders refused, pointing to Cyrus's order, and the book calls these neighbors enemies, though readers debate how much the refusal itself fueled what followed.

parts.label: Years of pressure (vv. 4-5)
parts.note: The local population discouraged the builders and paid officials to block their plans. This went on from the reign of Cyrus to that of Darius, roughly 538 to 520 BC.

parts.label: Complaints under later kings (vv. 6-7)
parts.note: The writer jumps ahead decades to the reigns of Xerxes and Artaxerxes, grouping events by theme rather than by date. From verse 8 the book switches into Aramaic, the official language of the Persian empire, and stays in it through 6:18.

parts.label: The letter against Jerusalem (vv. 8-16)
parts.note: Officials based in Samaria warn the king that if Jerusalem's walls go up, the city will rebel and stop paying taxes, so this letter concerns the walls, not the temple. Their claim of loyalty in verse 14 rests on an old idiom, literally eating the palace's salt, meaning the king paid their keep.

parts.label: The king orders a halt (vv. 17-23)
parts.note: Royal records showed that Jerusalem had revolted against earlier empires and once had powerful kings of its own, so the king ordered the work stopped until he gave further orders (v. 21). That condition left room for the later permission described in the book of Nehemiah, but for now the officials enforced the halt at once by force.

parts.label: Back to the temple (v. 24)
parts.note: The writer returns to the original story: work on the temple stood still until the second year of King Darius, about 520 BC. The next chapter picks up from there.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the leaders' refusal of help in verse 3 was a faithful act of protecting pure worship or an exclusion that hardened a long and bitter division between neighbors.
think: When a community works to protect what matters most to it, where do you think the line falls between guarding its identity and shutting others out?
